title: Passover: the week of matzah
hookLine: a week of eating the bread of affliction and freedom
tomorrow: seven weeks of counting. counting what?

cards: Snap. That's the sound a sheet of matzah makes, dry and sharp, and by the third day of Passover some people are tired of hearing it. A cracker with no rise and nothing to hide behind.
And the seder gives this one flat bread two names that pull in opposite directions. Near the start, it's the bread of affliction. Later, it's the bread of the night they walked out.
Same box. So which is it, sad or free?

teach.b: Deuteronomy names it in one verse: "seven days shalt thou eat unleavened bread therewith, even the bread of affliction; for in haste didst thou come forth out of the land of Egypt." Listen to the two halves. Affliction.
And haste. The verse already holds both.
The Haggadah lifts the matzah early in the night and says, in Aramaic, this is the bread of poverty our ancestors ate in Egypt; then, right away, let all who are hungry come and eat.
Exodus tells the other side: "they baked unleavened cakes of the dough which they brought forth out of Egypt, for it was not leavened; because they were thrust out of Egypt, and could not tarry."

No time for the dough to rise, because the door opened all at once. In the Mishnah, Rabban Gamliel says matzah is one of the things a seder has to explain, and the Haggadah's answer is that second story.
So the same bread is both. Flat because slaves ate what was cheap and quick. Flat because people leaving in a hurry can't wait for dough.
The taste doesn't change. The story you tell with it does. That's what a week of matzah can be: not enduring a cracker, but tasting the turn from one story to the other, bite by bite.

how: During the week of Passover, Jews who keep it eat matzah instead of leavened bread; at the seder the matzah is lifted and called the bread of affliction, and later explained as the bread that had no time to rise.

games.q: one bread, two stories — tap the pairs.

s: it's the bread of affliction and also the bread that had no time to rise when they left.
the bread of affliction passage in the Haggadah ends with an invitation
this is the bread of poverty; let all who are hungry come and eat.

games.q: day three of Passover. your little brother pushes his matzah away: it tastes like cardboard and it's sad. what could you tell him?
o: it's also the bread of leaving: no time to rise, because they got out fast.
it's sad on purpose; this week is only for remembering the suffering.
it's just a rule for the week; eat it and don't think about why.
games.why: the same bread is both, affliction and haste, in one verse of Deuteronomy. a week of matzah turns one story into the other.

practice: Take a piece of matzah, or any plain cracker you have. Break it near your ear and listen to the snap, then eat one small bite slowly, with nothing on it. With the first bite, think: bread of affliction.
With the next, think: bread of people who left in a hurry.

wordCard.voice: Passover: the festival of the exodus, eaten a week at a time as matzah, one flat bread with two stories.

orig.note: Hebrew: unleavened bread, flat because there was no time to rise.

carryVoice: Keep this: bread of freedom, the same flat bread as the bread of affliction, told the other way. That's the day.
